Steven Spielberg has always been the master of awe and his new film Disclosure Day is no exception. If only he trusted his intuition.

Steven Spielberg’s Disclosure Day begins with a literal punch in the face. The opening scenes of the film have a kinetic rush: with minimal exposition, we are introduced to Daniel Kellner (Josh O’Connor) and his girlfriend, Jane Blankenship (Eve Hewson), who are being held hostage.

The crisp nocturnal cinematography by Janusz Kamiński and Sarah Broshar’s brisk editing recall the paranoid landscapes of the Mission: Impossible films and Christopher Nolan’s noir fantasies, yet the seamlessly classical mise en scène is undeniably the work of Spielberg. It’s as if the septuagenarian director is daring the audience, wanting to make it clear he is far from over the hill.

Daniel is on the run from his former employer Wardex, a shadowy security organisation with links to the FBI. For decades Wardex has been involved in covering up evidence of extraterrestrial contact. Daniel and a handful of his colleagues have come across damning evidence of the merciless interrogation and torture of aliens. This renegade group of rebels, led by Hugo Wakefield (Colman Domingo), want to unleash their trove of recorded evidence to the world. Wardex’s attempt to sabotage their disclosure, led by Noah Scanlon (Colin Firth), forms the narrative spine of the film.

The visceral excitement of the filmmaking is too often let down by the heavy-handedness of the script. The screenplay is by David Koepp, who wrote one of Spielberg’s most successful films, Jurassic Park (1993), but it’s tone-deaf when it comes to dialogue. After Daniel and Jane have made their escape, they find haven among Catholic nuns. Jane was a novitiate when she was younger and when Daniel reveals why Wardex is chasing them, her reaction is to doubt the readiness of the world to hear we are not the supreme beings in the universe. Her arguments are banal and Daniel’s response is equally trite. The writing is so shallow you can sense O’Connor and Hewson straining to build a rapport: their relationship never feels believable.

Disclosure Day raises questions of doubt and existential meaning but too often the playing out of these tensions is reduced to mawkishness and a strained Christian mysticism. The film’s most effective moments are those that reveal the anguish of the aliens. When Daniel first shows Jane recordings of Wardex’s cruelty to the extraterrestrials, Spielberg keeps the visuals and sound elliptical and doesn’t linger over the images. His restraint underscores his talent and responsiveness as a filmmaker: the effect is shocking. After the powerful impact of such scenes, returning to another car chase or more of Noah’s cat-and-mouse pursuit of the fugitives becomes exasperating.

When Spielberg concentrates on the story’s central question – how we might approach other alien beings with empathy – the film comes close to achieving beauty.

Thankfully the film has Emily Blunt. She plays Margaret Fairchild, a Kansas City TV weather presenter who is always hoping for a better job, a better life to come along. When a northern cardinal swoops into the apartment she shares with her boyfriend, she looks at the bird and suddenly can speak in perfect Russian. Margaret, like Daniel, had an encounter with the extraterrestrials when she was a child, an experience she has repressed. Her strange new powers will prove central to the success or failure of the renegades’ attempts to outmanoeuvre Wardex and expose their cover-up.

There’s an element of the ridiculous in the onset and scale of Margaret’s emerging superpowers, yet Blunt is such a capable performer she can play both the comedy and apprehension in her character’s inexplicable transformation. When we first meet Margaret, she is a ruthless woman on the make. Her character softens as the story progresses, yet the toughness that Blunt reveals in her first few scenes is never completely sacrificed. Her ability to combine humour with stubbornness is a rare talent: her likeability always feels earnt. We don’t ever feel she’s sucking up to us. She keeps us invested in Disclosure Day even at its most ludicrous or sentimental.

Initially I was unconvinced by Josh O’Connor’s performance. His thoughtfulness, his almost reticent screen persona, seemed at odds with the action tropes of the film’s opening act. Once Daniel is saved by Margaret, O’Connor visibly relaxes as an actor. Blunt’s control seems to act as a tonic and allows O’Connor to reveal Daniel’s vulnerability – he still possesses a core of childlike awe. The idea he’s prepared to sabotage his security because he has witnessed another being’s suffering suddenly makes sense.

The rendering of awe has always been a pivotal part of Spielberg’s filmmaking. Disclosure Day isn’t necessarily a sequel to his early masterwork Close Encounters of the Third Kind (1977), but undoubtedly there are echoes and resonances with that earlier film and his wondrous fantasia E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (1982). These connections are consciously embedded in the film in the lighting and design, particularly in two key scenes that directly refer to one of the most haunting sequences in all of Spielberg’s oeuvre, where the child is taken up by aliens in Close Encounters. It’s impossible not to be reminded of the chilling scenes of E.T.’s capture by government agents when we glimpse the footage of the Wardex agents interrogating and experimenting on the aliens in Disclosure Day.

There’s too much going on in this film, as if the filmmakers never quite trust the simplicity of the story they wanted to tell. That anxiety is reflected in John Williams’ self-derivative score, which becomes increasingly bombastic. The supporting cast can’t do anything with their roles, which are lazily sketched and written. There’s also a desultory subplot about the possible outbreak of a world war, although we never sense any real threat of nuclear Armageddon.

When Spielberg concentrates on the story’s central question – how we might approach other alien beings with empathy – the film comes close to achieving beauty. There is a real power in the final disclosure, where we see how the world might respond to such a revelation. It’s fantastical – even absurd – but as with Close Encounters of the Third Kind, Jurassic Park and E.T., there’s a real pleasure in giving ourselves over to wonderment. Being reminded of the awe one felt as a child at the hope for magic and fantasy is no small thing. It’s one of Spielberg’s greatest gifts as a filmmaker.

Spielberg has nothing to prove. Four years ago he directed The Fabelmans, one of his greatest films. It’s an autobiographical film about a young man discovering his vocation for film, and its elegiac and humane script was co-written with Tony Kushner. Spielberg and Kushner collaborated on 2012’s Lincoln, a film of great ambition but formal inconsistency. The Fabelmans left behind the grand sweep of history and mined the essence of what ignites inspiration and how talent is both shaped and compromised by familial loyalty and conflict, to create a tender, mature work. I don’t think a young person could have looked back so forensically on the pain visited on a child by divorce yet been so unequivocally generous to both parents. It is remarkably free of bitterness – the work of filmmakers who trusted their story and intuition.

The opening scene of The Fabelmans is of the young director-to-be being taken to his first film, Cecil B. DeMille’s overblown epic The Greatest Show on Earth. The child becomes obsessed with how the director managed to convincingly show a train colliding with a car on screen. In that child’s working out of how to achieve those effects we see the emergence of filmmaking instinct and talent.

Spielberg is still trying to make The Greatest Show on Earth. In the final scenes of Disclosure Day, he almost gets there. Yet that first experience might be as much a millstone as it is an inspiration: Disclosure Day doesn’t need the train crash, the car chases, the implausible shoot-’em-up games. They mar its effectiveness and compromise its story. This film is a very particular kind of failure: the work of a great filmmaker trying to second-guess himself.

I’m not alone in considering The Fabelmans a great film, but it was a commercial flop. It’s possible that, even after all these years, that box-office failure spooked Spielberg. Maybe it’s the price that comes with chasing popular success. In trying to please everyone, you forget how to listen to your instincts.

Disclosure Day is screening in cinemas nationally.
